comparison: Both evaluate UKBB dataset characteristics and limitations (C1-C4, C67, C85-C88). OpenEval focuses on dataset description and selection bias acknowledgment, while peer review emphasizes acceptance of data limitations as common caveats for human studies. Both find claims SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R24 addresses data quality and exclusion criteria (C85-C88), which peer review R1 incorporates as part of broader dataset limitations discussion. Both accept the handling procedures as reasonable.
OpenEval R23 discusses cross-sectional design limitations (C67-C68), partially overlapping with peer review R1's acceptance of dataset limitations. Peer review R1 also includes C67 in its evaluation.

Both address the constant aging rate assumption (C68). OpenEval acknowledges it as a simplification inherent to UKBB structure, while peer review accepts it as a reasonable modeling choice given data constraints. Both find it SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate multi-system modeling findings (C12, C78-C81, C101). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of model performance and component analysis, while peer review explicitly praises the finding that multi-system input improves prediction. Both SUPPORTED, with peer review noting this 'makes scenes in general.'
OpenEval R3 addresses model performance metrics (C13-C14, C89-C90), which peer review R2 implicitly accepts by not questioning RMSE and R² values. Both find metrics reasonable and SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R25 discusses phenotype clustering patterns (C106-C108), which peer review R2 does not explicitly address but implicitly accepts as part of the comprehensive data-driven approach.

Both evaluate ΔAge validation metrics (C15-C16, C69-C70). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation with caution about p-value interpretation, while peer review accepts these as part of 'convincing' results without challenge. Both SUPPORTED.

Both address mortality validation (C17-C19, C91-C94). OpenEval emphasizes the strength of Gompertzian patterns and independence from model training, while peer review implicitly accepts mortality predictions as convincing. Both SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R6 includes mortality statistics (C17-C18), which peer review R20 addresses separately, accepting these descriptive statistics as part of mortality validation. Both SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate parental longevity associations (C21-C24). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation and heritability context, while peer review accepts these as validation that the model captures heritable aging components. Both SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R15 discusses genetic correlation with parental mortality (C57), which peer review R4 implicitly includes in accepting parental lifespan correlations as validation. Both SUPPORTED.

Perfect overlap on education findings (C35-C37). OpenEval emphasizes statistical strength while cautioning against causal inference, peer review identifies this as a novel finding without challenging causality claims. Both SUPPORTED.

Perfect overlap on computer gaming findings (C41-C43, C63, C97). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to concerns about reverse causation and need for experimental validation, while peer review rates SUPPORTED and explicitly identifies it as a novel discovery without skepticism. Key disagreement on certainty level.

Both evaluate GWAS results and quality control (C44-C49, C53-C54). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of inflation factors and heritability estimates, peer review accepts findings as 'convincing' and notes identification of known and new factors. Both SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R14 addresses heritability estimates (C53-C54), which peer review R7 implicitly accepts as part of overall GWAS validation. Both SUPPORTED.

Perfect overlap on nervous system/synapse biology findings (C58-C59, C96). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but urges caution due to marginal significance and GO annotation biases, peer review rates SUPPORTED and explicitly identifies as novel discovery. Both accept but OpenEval more cautious.

Both evaluate CST3 marker vs driver distinction using cluster-dropout analysis (C60-C62, C113-C114). OpenEval provides detailed methodological validation and cites supporting MR studies, peer review accepts the approach as part of 'comprehensive data-driven approaches.' Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R28 discusses disease associations and MR findings (C109-C112) that support the marker/driver distinction, which peer review R9 implicitly accepts through overall positive assessment. Both SUPPORTED.

Both address cross-cohort GWAS comparisons (C73-C77). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on statistical significance of overlaps, peer review rates UNCERTAIN due to lack of complete external validation dataset. Key disagreement: OpenEval accepts partial validation, peer review wants full model validation.

Perfect overlap on reduced 12-trait model (C84). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with note that prospective validation needed, peer review rates UNCERTAIN explicitly requesting external biobank validation. Both identify need for additional validation but differ on current support level.

Perfect overlap on robustness across analytical methods (C82-C83, C102-C105). OpenEval provides detailed comparison of PLS, linear regression, and GBM concordance, peer review accepts without challenge as part of comprehensive approach. Both SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate socioeconomic and lifestyle factors (C25-C26, C29-C31). OpenEval emphasizes consistency with established literature, peer review accepts as identifying environmental factors impacting aging. Both SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R9 addresses alcohol consumption findings (C32-C34), which peer review R13 implicitly includes in broader environmental associations evaluation. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R11 addresses leisure activities (C38-C40), which peer review R13 includes in environmental factors evaluation. OpenEval cautions against causal inference, peer review accepts as novel findings. Both SUPPORTED.
Perfect overlap on air pollution cluster-dropout analysis (C64-C66). OpenEval notes residual association below Bonferroni threshold, peer review accepts methodology without challenge. Both SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate genetic correlations distinguishing drivers from markers (C55-C56). OpenEval provides detailed interpretation of differential correlations, peer review implicitly accepts through overall positive assessment. Both SUPPORTED.

Perfect overlap on APOE age-independent effects (C71-C72, C115). OpenEval notes mechanisms are speculative but finding is important, peer review accepts without challenge as part of identifying known factors. Both SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R2 addresses age-related physiological trends (C10-C11), which peer review R17 includes as basic validation that model captures known aging biology. Both SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R26 discusses phenotypes not in model that still correlate with ΔAge (C27-C28), which peer review R17 implicitly accepts as external validation. Both SUPPORTED.
Both address prior work context (C5-C9). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of literature summary accuracy, peer review implicitly accepts as accurate background. Both SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R28 discusses disease associations from literature (C50-C52, C109-C112), which peer review R18 implicitly accepts as contextual claims. Both SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R29 addresses general aging biology background (C98-C100), which peer review R18 implicitly accepts as accurate context. Both SUPPORTED.
